strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: quadratic complexity of attention in long-sequence video generation is a genuine bottleneck for deployment
Data-free post-training approach avoids need for curated datasets, significantly more practical than prior linear attention methods requiring expensive pretraining

Well-motivated technical contributions with clear empirical validation: selective transfer elegantly frames layer selection as binary classification, and ADM objective is intuitive in matching distributions across entire trajectory

Comprehensive ablation studies and experimental validation demonstrate necessity of each component (Tables 2-4, Figs. 3, 8); good analysis of training efficiency showing 4.4× speedup vs. auxiliary model approaches

Strong empirical results on tested model: 1.43× speedup maintained with negligible quality drop (Table 1); 15.92× speedup with 4-step distillation; outperforms or matches concurrent sparse attention baselines (SVG2, XAttn)
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Fig. 1-5) effectively communicating the approach and results
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Evaluation on only a single model (Wan 1.3B) severely undermines generalization claims; no experiments on CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, or other contemporary architectures; impossible to assess whether layer selections and method transfer across models
Speedup gains are modest (1.43× typical, 1.25-2.00× range) and incremental relative to existing sparse attention and linear attention literature; not transformative for deployment

Lack of mechanistic understanding of why method works: no explanation for why certain layers (e.g., layer 1) are critical to preserve, no analysis of architectural properties determining replaceability, purely empirical observations

Technical choices insufficiently justified: mixed-attention formulation (Eq. 8) presented without exploring alternatives; constraint loss (Eq. 9) uses simple L2 penalty without ablating L1 or soft constraints; Fig. 3 shows r still fluctuates despite Lreg, suggesting optimization challenges

ADM objective justification is limited: claims about temporal artifacts (flicker, jitter) relegated to Appendix without main-paper evidence; comparison to naive MSE may conflate distribution-matching benefits with implementation differences; using uθ for score computation is pragmatic but differs from standard practice with no isolated ablation

Generalization concerns unaddressed: no sensitivity analysis for number of collected samples; unknown whether diverse prompts affect layer selection; scalability to different video lengths/resolutions/frame rates untested; no evidence layer selections transfer across models
Concurrent work SLA proposes similar selective replacement (intra-layer vs. inter-layer distinction); claimed orthogonality for combination lacks experimental validation, reducing novelty

Overclaiming and imprecision: ~1% performance drop contradicts 'lossless acceleration' claim; 'first efficient data-free post-training' overlooks SLA's post-training approach; VBench-only evaluation limits assessment of perceptual quality despite qualitative claims

Missing critical ablations: no isolated evaluation of ADM vs. Lmse/LDMD controlling for implementation details; sensitivity to hyperparameter λ unexpectedly low (~1%); α annealing schedule appears ad-hoc
Reproducibility concerns: code availability unmentioned; hyperparameter choices (λ=0.01) lack justification; training with fluctuating r around 0.5 may suffer from instability

Data-free post-training approach that leverages model's own outputs, avoiding need for curated video datasets
Clear empirical observation that different layers have varying replaceability (Figure 2), motivating selective transfer
Anytime distribution matching objective is a reasonable contribution that aligns distributions across full sampling trajectory
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Reasonable experimental design with VBench and VBench-2.0 evaluation
Well-written paper with clear visualizations of the framework
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines standard techniques (mixed attention with learnable weights, STE, distribution matching) without fundamental innovations
Speedup gains (1.25-2.00×) are modest and comparable to existing sparse-attention baselines shown in Figure 6, contradicting superiority claims
Severely limited experimental scope: only tested on single model (Wan 1.3B); no evaluation on CogVideoX, SANA-Video, or other architectures despite mentioning them
No empirical comparison with recent linear attention methods (SANA-Video, LinGen, M4V) despite claiming 'first efficient data-free' approach
Quality preservation claims overstated: Table 1 shows marginal or negative differences vs. baseline on individual metrics; 4-step model shows ~1% degradation
Critical technical concern in Equation 8: mixed attention during training but switching at inference creates distribution shift; Figure 3 shows regularization is essential, indicating fragile design
Unclear contribution of intermediate timestep matching: Table 4 shows w/ ŝ†_t variant only 0.46 points lower, suggesting auxiliary model difference may not be primary factor
Missing rigorous justification: why intermediate timestep matching fundamentally preserves capacity better than matching at t=0 only
Regularization term (Lreg) with annealing schedule appears ad-hoc without principled design explanation or ablation on schedule choices
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned, annealing schedule for α incompletely specified, target selection strategy not principled
Limited generalization analysis: no evaluation across model scales, video lengths (>5s), resolutions, or different architectures
Computational cost of training not reported; 3K steps on 8 H100s is substantial but not contextualized
Score function derivation (Eq. 13) assumes rectified flow holds during training, but model continuously changes—assumption not validated
Ablation in Table 4 insufficient: cannot isolate contribution of intermediate timestep matching vs. using model itself for score estimation

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the quadratic attention complexity bottleneck in video diffusion models with practical importance; the observation that different layers have significantly different replaceability is valuable and non-obvious

Novel selective transfer mechanism that intelligently automates layer selection via learnable binary classification scores with proper regularization (L_con, L_reg) to prevent optimization instability

Anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is well-motivated, addressing limitations of naive MSE (temporal artifacts) and few-step distillation (ignoring intermediate timesteps); efficiently uses the current model to estimate its own score function, avoiding 4.4× auxiliary training cost
Data-free post-training paradigm is practical and deployable without requiring large curated video datasets; training data extracted from pre-trained model's own trajectory

Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple baselines (SVG, SVG2, XAttn, DFA), evaluation on both VBench and VBench-2.0 with 8+ quality dimensions, and thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4) isolating individual component contributions
Strong empirical results maintaining or exceeding baseline quality while achieving 1.43× speedup on full model; 15.92× speedup with minimal quality drop after 4-step distillation
Clear presentation with precise mathematical formulation; effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and well-structured ablations that rigorously support design choices
weaknesses: Limited model scope: evaluation only on Wan 1.3B undermines generalization claims; unknown whether layer replaceability patterns generalize to CogVideoX, other architectures, or different model designs; abstract claims applicability to 'video DMs' broadly but evidence is narrow

Speedup gains are modest (1.43×) for the linearization method alone without specialized kernel implementation, which significantly limits practical deployment impact; only 53% of layers replaced (16/30), meaning attention still contributes substantial computational cost

4-step distillation results (15.92× speedup) conflate multiple techniques; unclear attribution between linearization and distillation components; appendix indicates direct few-step distillation of linear attention causes catastrophic failures, suggesting distillation difficulty is not well-understood

Incomplete theoretical understanding of why certain layers are more replaceable; Figure 2 shows empirical patterns but mechanistic explanation is shallow; hypothesis that 'errors by shallow layers are compensated by later layers' is intuitive but unvalidated

ADM objective lacks rigorous theoretical justification for why trajectory-wide distribution matching outperforms final-distribution matching; assumption that û_θ reliably estimates ŝ_t during training needs stronger support; ODE solver choice (Euler) used for 'simplicity' without sensitivity analysis

Experimental design concerns: sparse attention baselines may be sub-optimally tuned compared to highly-optimized FlashAttention2; excluding 'auxiliary designs' from baselines could unfairly penalize them; unclear how much quality gain is architectural vs. from regularization/training improvements

Limited evaluation scope: only text-to-video generation; no image-to-video, conditional variants, or other tasks; memory efficiency not discussed despite being equally important as latency; no perceptual studies or user evaluations beyond VBench metrics

Incomplete related work comparison: concurrent SLA method [63] not compared directly; pre-training methods (SANA-Video, LinGen) excluded with acknowledgment but without providing relative context; unclear advantages vs. simply applying selective transfer + ADM to SLA

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: λ tested only in narrow range; annealing schedule for α in L_reg not detailed; target=16 choice justified empirically but lacks principled justification; would benefit from more systematic sensitivity analysis

Notation and presentation issues: u_θ for velocity prediction is non-standard; mixed-attention inference behavior (Eq. 8) could be clearer regarding deterministic r rounding; some key details (temporal artifact examples) relegated to appendix

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the O(n²) attention bottleneck in video diffusion models with practical relevance
Novel selective transfer mechanism using learnable parameters r to automatically determine and progressively convert layers to linear attention

Anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is a meaningful contribution that matches distributions across entire sampling trajectory, not just final samples; cleverly avoids auxiliary models by self-estimating score functions
Data-free post-training approach is practical given limited access to large curated video datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two model scales, two resolutions, 8 VBench dimensions plus VBench-2.0, with thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Consistent empirical improvements over sparse attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttention) with outperformance on several metrics (Overall/Scene Consistency)
Strong 4-step distilled results achieving 15.9-20.9× speedup with only ~1-3% performance degradation; visual quality well-preserved
Technical soundness with proper mathematical formulations, correct derivations in appendix, and appropriate use of standard techniques (STE)
Clear presentation with effective figures (especially Fig. 2 demonstrating layer replaceability variance and Fig. 3 showing Lreg importance)
weaknesses: Incremental speedup improvements (1.43-1.71×) compared to sparsification baselines (1.15-1.42×), limiting practical impact for a method claiming to solve critical efficiency bottleneck; further gains require unimplemented specialized kernel optimizations

Insufficient theoretical analysis of why layer replaceability varies dramatically (Fig. 2); explanation that 'errors from shallow layers compensated by subsequent layers' is intuitive but not rigorously justified
Evaluated only on Wan models; generalization to other SOTA architectures (CogVideoX, different depths, MoE designs) is unvalidated despite practical importance

Requires pre-specifying target parameter (number of layers to replace); no principled method to choose target for new models, limiting usability; Table 2 shows significant degradation beyond target=18 for 1.3B
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work (SLA); claims about orthogonality between inter-layer and intra-layer mixing are unvalidated
ADM design choices lack strong justification: using model being trained (uˆθ) for sˆt estimation could create circular dependencies; no ablations on numerical solver or timestep sensitivity
High computational requirements (8-32× H100 GPUs) with unclear absolute training time; data collection phase cost not quantified, limiting accessibility
Pattern of selected layers {2-8, 10-13, 15-16, 23, 25, 30} is not analyzed; no investigation of consistency principles or depth-dependent selectability patterns
Missing ablations: only one linear attention kernel tested (Hedgehog), no exploration of hybrid sparse-linear approaches, limited exploration of λ hyperparameter
Generalization concerns unaddressed: will selective transfer patterns transfer to different architectures? Does model-specific optimization affect layer selection reproducibility?
